props.title: The Skydivers

sections.content: The Skydivers stands as one of Coleman Francis's most notorious contributions to cinematic infamy, alongside Beast of Yucca Flats (1961) and Red Zone Cuba (1966). Shot in stark black-and-white with Francis's trademark incompetent direction, it's a mesmerizing disaster that attempts to blend skydiving footage with a melodramatic love triangle. The film gained legendary status through Mystery Science Theater 3000 (1988-1999), which brilliantly skewered its endless coffee-drinking scenes, mumbled dialogue, and baffling plot developments.

sections.content: The "so bad it's good" genre flourished in the 1960s, with regional filmmakers operating far outside Hollywood's quality controls. The Creeping Terror (1964) featured a monster clearly made from carpet scraps, while Monster A-Go-Go (1965) baffled viewers with its incoherent plot and shocking non-ending. These films share The Skydivers' fundamental production issues: poor sound recording, amateur actors reading from cue cards, and editing that defies basic continuity. SUBHEAD: The Coleman Francis Trilogy

Francis's three directorial efforts form a fascinating study in consistent incompetence. Each film features his obsession with light aircraft, coffee consumption, and characters speaking in barely audible mumbles. Beast of Yucca Flats (1961) never syncs dialogue with actors' lips, while Red Zone Cuba (1966) drags viewers through an endless series of poorly staged fights and inexplicable plot turns. The Skydivers sits between them, combining Francis's worst tendencies with genuinely dangerous skydiving stunts.
